newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australia govt revives push for new tax.
newsitem.headline: Australia govt revives push for new tax.

text.p: The Australian government on Tuesday pressed for a major overhaul of the tax system, reviving the push for a controversial goods and services tax that many blame for delaying the conservatives' return to power.
Treasurer Peter Costello said taxation needed reform to reduce the tax burden and make Australia more competitive within the Asia-Pacific region.
"We think that it is important that we keep focussing on reforming the Australian taxation system," Costello told reporters in the southern city of Adelaide.
"We are starting to look at new challenges, rolling towards our goal of a low-tax, fair, decent Australian economy."
He would not rule out a future goods and services tax (GST).
"It's far too early to start speculating about specific outcomes," he said.
The Liberal-National coalition ended 13 years of Labor rule in March, 1996, after dropping its policy of imposing a 15-percent value-added tax that many believe robbed it of victory in 1993.
Prime Minister John Howard ruled out a GST in his first three year term, but said at the weekend said the tax system needed reform. Howard would not rule out a GST in later terms.
A consumption tax, or value-added tax, is paid by consumers when they buy a good or service.
The Labor opposition firmed its opposition to a consumption tax on Tuesday, criticising it as unfair and saying unemployment was a bigger problem than taxes.
"It's inherently unfair for lower income earners and not very flash for middle income earners or small business as well," Labor treasury spokesman Gareth Evans said in a radio interview.
"No design any of us has ever seen for a GST overcomes these problems -- I don't think they ever will.
'Let's get it clear. The tax system is not the first order problem in Australia at the moment. Jobs are the problem."
Australia's unemployment rate has remain stuck above 8.5 percent since the government won power and is only expected to fall to 8.25 percent, year average, in fiscal 1997/98.
Evans had appeared to soften Labor's opposition to a consumption tax when he said on Monday the opposition would consider a GST if a fair system could be worked out.
But he said he had been misunderstood and was pointing out a fair GST was impossible.
Business and welfare groups have called for a consumption tax and polls have shown rising support for such a tax as part of an overhaul for the country's complex indirect tax system.
Most groups acknowledge the introduction of a consumption tax would have to be accompanied by reforms to ease the impact on welfare recipients and low income earners.

"You've got to go into the social security system and look at those categories of people for whom everyday purchases are a larger proportion of their spending than for the rest of us who are more well off," former tax commissioner Trevor Boucher said.
